newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seems unbeatable after rocky start.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seems unbeatable after rocky start.

text.p: President Bill Clinton rebounded from a chaotic first two years in office, marked by disasters personal and political, to regain the confidence of voters and position himself for re-election.

Grayer and sobered by four years of swiftly changing fortunes, the 50-year-old Democratic "baby-boomer" nonetheless displayed a boyish optimism and limitless energy that infected crowds all along the campaign trail.

He set the tone for his re-election drive at the start of the year in his annual State of the Union speech, portraying himself as the leader of the mainstream political centre and proclaiming: "The era of big government is over."

As the year progressed he co-opted many Republican issues -- welfare reform and crime-fighting for example -- to run as a conservative Democrat. But perhaps most noteworthy was the way he turned to his own advantage the pledge of Republican rival Bob Dole that, at 73, Dole was "a bridge to the past" of traditional values.

Calling himself the candidate for the 21st century, Clinton would say at his rallies: "Are we going to build a bridge to the future or a bridge to the past?" It managed to remind voters indirectly of Dole's advanced age.

As recently as late 1994, Clinton seemed destined to be a mediocre one-term president as Republicans rode a wave of voter discontent to take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives for the first time in 40 years.
Clinton was reduced to defending himself publicly against accusations that he had become "irrelevant."

But then Republicans handed him a free ride back from the political wilderness, pushing national spending cuts many people viewed as too harsh for the poor and elderly and too rough on education and environmental protections.

If Clinton had trouble making people believe he had core convictions, the Republicans gave him something to be against. Since he had never really stopped campaigning after his 1992 victory, he was off and running against "the extremists" in control of Congress.

His message, poll-tested and adapted to an America largely tired of Washington's ever-growing bureacratic tentacles, was that the federal government should be reduced but was too important to cede all control to state and local governments.

"Are we going to tell the American people, 'you're on your own,' or are we going to say that, yes, it does take a village to raise and educate our children and build our country and go forward together?" he would say.
Clinton was mired in controversy as soon as the elation of his January 1993 inauguration faded.

There was the firing of White House travel office workers, the issue of his opening the military to homosexuals, several botched appointments to key positions and accusations about the Clintons' Whitewater investment from the 1980s in Arkansas.
The darkest hour came in July 1993 when his boyhood friend from Arkansas, deputy White House counsel Vince Foster, drove out to a Northern Virginia park and shot himself to death.

The after-shocks still ripple through the White House. And independent counsel Kenneth Starr's Whitewater investigation is still going strong, guaranteeing pressures from that quarter will continue in a second Clinton term.

A plan for a radical revamping of the U.S. health care system, led by Clinton's wife, Hillary, fed into suspicions Clinton was at heart a big-government liberal and became the biggest political disaster of his first term.

Many Americans surveyed in polls said they had questions about Clinton's character and did not entirely trust him, but the question marks were not enough to keep him from piling up a large lead over Dole in the months before the election.

Talkative and supremely self-confident, Clinton was the kind of fellow who stirred strong emotions both positive and negative. This was exemplified during a recent jog on a California beach when he was denounced by one woman as a "yellow-bellied, draft-dodging liar" and hailed by another as a protector of children. "We love you," she said.

Clinton was also blessed by plenty of good luck in his campaign, in the form of a prosperous U.S. economy. Many analysts said this was the cyclical product of various forces but he attributed it to his own economic policies -- never mentioning they included a huge tax increase.
"We are better off than we were four years ago," he said.
Abroad, Clinton was unafraid to project U.S. military might, sending forces to Bosnia, Somalia, Haiti and the Gulf.

He worked on developing personal relationships with world leaders with mixed success. For instance, the assassination of his friend Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin led to Shimon Peres taking over. Clinton backed Peres for re-election only to watch in dismay as right-winger Benjamin Netanyahu won.
Born on Aug. 19, 1946, in tiny Hope, Arkansas, Clinton got a taste of -- and for -- the presidency with a group of teenagers who met President John Kennedy at the White House.

In high school, he tooled around in a big Buick and pretended he was Elvis Presley. He later avoided the Vietnam War draft by using student advantages, attended Georgetown University, was a Rhodes Scholar at Oxford in the late 1960s and took a law degree at Yale. He met Hillary there.
Their daughter, Chelsea, is 16.

Clinton won his first election in 1976 as attorney general of Arkansas. Two years later, at 32, he became America's youngest state governor and held that post through most of the 1980s and into the early 1990s, gaining national limelight.
